title: Approve an invoice: pick the APPROVED rubber stamp by its label, ink it, hold the sheet, stamp squarely in the box
context: Almost everyone has stamped paper or watched it done: a PAID or date stamp at a shop counter, a due date in a library book, a parcel at the post office, a passport, a child's ink-stamp set. People judge the result at a glance: the right stamp, a clean whole print, square, inside its box. Office and mail-room staff still do it daily. For a robot it is harder than it looks: the stamps look alike and differ only by a printed word; a stamp works only after a second step, a press on the ink pad; a legible print needs a real press of about 5 to 20 N with the die flat on the paper, square and inside a 5 cm box; the loose invoice book slides unless the other hand holds it; and a wrong stamp on a document cannot be undone. Here an A5 invoice book lies loose on a desk pad, the approval box of its top invoice empty. A rack holds three wooden rubber stamps labelled REJECTED (red), APPROVED (green) and COPY (blue); an open ink pad lies beside it. The instruction names neither the stamp nor the box.
setup: Counter top is z = 0.7475 m; positions are in metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left. All real size; shapes are CAD models. (1) Desk pad, fixed: dark green leatherette, 300 (x) x 460 (y) x 2 mm, centre (0.37, 0.10). (2) Invoice book, free: an A5 pad of invoices glued at its top edge, 148 x 210 x 4 mm, about 90 g, lying loose on the desk pad, centre (0.345, 0.07), long side along x; its top invoice (called the sheet below) has its text reading toward -y (left to right as seen from the robot), top of the page at the far edge; printed header, four item lines with amounts, a total, and at its near right corner an empty box 50 x 50 mm headed APPROVAL, centre (0.280, 0.033). (3) Stamp rack, fixed: walnut tray 150 (x) x 76 (y) x 12 mm at (0.40, -0.185) with three felt-lined pockets 32 x 56 mm. (4) Three wooden rubber stamps, free, standing in the pockets at x = 0.354, 0.400, 0.446, y = -0.185: each 75 mm tall, about 60 g, rubber face 20 (x) x 44 (y) mm, wooden mount 26 x 50 mm, handle 24 x 46 mm with a flat top carrying a coloured label 20 x 42 mm with white capitals 7.5 mm tall, facing straight up and reading from the robot's left to its right: nearest REJECTED (red), middle APPROVED (green), farthest COPY (blue). The words are legible in the overview picture and from a wrist camera within about 15 cm; in the 640-pixel top camera the labels are told apart by colour and position, the words are too small to read there. Apart from the label they are identical. The printed word runs along the long side of the face, the same way round as the label. (5) Ink pad, fixed: blue tin 70 (x) x 110 (y) mm at (0.275, -0.310), lying open, its dark felt 64 x 104 mm standing 13 mm above the counter and giving up to 2 mm under a stamp (4 N per mm); its lid lies open behind it. (6) A ballpoint pen on the desk pad at (0.47, 0.255), dressing. Real trial props (all low cost): STAMPS: three made-to-order wooden-mount rubber stamps (any stamp shop) with a 20 x 44 mm rubber die on 2.5 mm foam, the words APPROVED, REJECTED and COPY each inside a 16 x 40 mm frame; mount and handle of planed beech, 50 x 26 mm foot, 24 x 46 mm handle, 75 mm tall overall, 60 g (+/- 10 g, kitchen scale); a paper label 20 x 42 mm glued on the handle top, white capitals 7.5 mm tall on green, red and blue, reading the same way round as the die. INK PAD: an ordinary felt office stamp pad in a hinged tin about 70 x 110 mm, black water-based ink, taped to the counter. PRESS FORCE: with this pad and paper the stamps must give a whole legible print at 5 to 20 N and only a faint or partial one under their own weight; check each stamp once per session on scrap paper lying on a kitchen scale (reading 0.5 to 2 kg), and inking should need a press of about 0.2 kg or more on the pad. INVOICE BOOK: the invoice layout printed 25 times on 80 g A5 paper, glued along the top edge to a 0.6 mm greyboard back (padding glue), 4 mm thick, about 90 g; on the desk pad it should start to slide at 0.3 to 0.5 N of sideways pull (spring scale). RACK: a 150 x 76 x 12 mm wooden block with three 32 x 56 mm pockets 6 mm deep, taped down. Positions are fixed with 3 mm masking tape: the desk pad's corners on the counter, and four L-shaped corner marks for the book on the desk pad, each with a second tick 10 mm outside it.
scoring: Read every step from measured contact forces, measured poses and the disclosed ink rule. The simulator's physics reports the contact force between each stamp and the invoice book and between each stamp and the ink pad's felt; nothing prints or inks by nearness alone. Ink: a stamp is inked once it stands on the felt (upright within 15 degrees, whole face on the felt) pressed with at least 2 N; resting there under its own weight (0.6 N) does not ink it; once inked it stays inked. Print: while an inked stamp's face touches the top invoice with a measured force of at least 0.2 N it leaves one mark, until it is lifted 3 mm clear: one press, one mark; a second press is a second mark. The mark is WHOLE, a legible impression, only if during that press the die lay flat on the page (all four corners of the face down) while the measured force was at least 5 N (an ordinary hand press is about 5 to 20 N; the peak is reported, nothing extra happens above 20 N). A lighter or tilted touch, including an inked stamp merely laid on the page under its own weight, leaves a faint or partial mark: it counts as a mark, as a freshly inked rubber really does leave one, but never as a whole one. A stamp held just above the page, or a dry stamp pressed however hard, leaves nothing. A mark's place and angle are the stamp's at the first moment the mark was whole; it is smeared if the stamp slid more than 4 mm over the page while touching. Marks are measured in the book's own frame, so they move with it. Any REJECTED or COPY mark on the invoice, whole or partial, at any time, scores 0 for the trial (latched); inking those stamps or printing them on the desk pad does not. Otherwise 0.5: an APPROVED mark whose centre is inside the approval box. 1.0: exactly one mark on the invoice, the APPROVED one, whole and not smeared, all four corners of its 40 x 16 mm outline inside the box, its text within 20 degrees of the page's text (not upside down), the invoice book left where it lay on the desk pad (all of it on the pad, moved less than 10 mm and turned less than 5 degrees), the other two stamps still standing in the rack, and the APPROVED stamp put down, not dropped, off the book (in the rack or on the desk, at rest, both grasp points at least 7 cm from its handle), all held 1 s. Two marks score at most 0.5. Doing nothing scores 0. Holding the book is not scored by itself: it is what keeps the box where the stamp is aimed and the book in its place when the stamp lands or lifts off askew. Reported: inked, ink_force_n (force on the felt when the stamp took ink), press_force_n (peak force of the press) and press_force_at_print_n (force at the moment the mark became whole), marks, mark_whole, mark_smear_mm, mark_offset_mm, mark_angle_deg, prints_off_sheet (inked stamps touched to the desk pad or counter), sheet_shift_mm, sheet_turn_deg, stamp_in_rack, dropped. Real trial: the same rule, read from the video and from a photo taken straight down on the book afterwards with a ruler lying beside the box (the printed box, 50 mm, is the scale). The ink on the paper is the evidence of a real press: a real stamp prints its whole frame and word legibly only when it has been inked on the pad and pressed flat with about 5 to 20 N (0.5 to 2 kg on a kitchen scale under the book; the judge checks the stamps this way before the session), so a whole, legible print is a whole mark and anything fainter or partial is a mark that is not whole. A mark is any visible ink print a stamp left on the top invoice, faint or partial included; which stamp made it is read from the video (label colour) and from the printed word. The zero is the moment a REJECTED or COPY print appears on the invoice; the starting state (clean invoice, dry stamps) is not a zero condition. 0.5: an APPROVED print whose frame centre is inside the box lines. 1.0: exactly one print on the invoice, the APPROVED one, its whole frame and every letter printed legibly (a real press, not a faint touch) and not dragged (no ghost edge wider than 4 mm), all four corners of its 40 x 16 mm frame inside the box lines, the frame's long side within 20 degrees of the box's lower line (protractor on the photo) and the word upright, every corner of the book still inside its 10 mm tick marks and its edge within 5 degrees of the tape, the other two stamps still standing in the rack, and the stamp put down by the hand (not dropped), standing or lying off the book with both grippers at least 7 cm from its handle for 1 s. A second visible print, however faint, is a second mark. A press with a dry stamp leaves nothing and costs nothing. Ink prints on the desk pad are noted, not scored.
reset_notes: Fixed starting poses, no randomisation; arms at the ready pose; all three stamps dry. Real trial reset: tear off the stamped invoice so the book shows a clean one (replace the book when it is under 3 mm thick); push the book into its four tape corners; blot every stamp on scrap paper until it leaves no print (a stamp is inked only by being pressed on the pad during the trial); stand the stamps in their pockets in the order REJECTED, APPROVED, COPY, labels reading toward the robot's right; open the ink pad. Ink pad: keep the tin closed between sessions, at room temperature; before each session make one test print on scrap paper with a spare stamp pressed at about 10 N (kitchen scale under the pad): it must be fully legible, otherwise re-ink the felt; re-ink after about 200 prints or one month; do not leave the tin open for more than 2 hours.
fidelity: PhysX 240 Hz, rigid bodies. Press force is the contact force PhysX reports between a stamp and the book or the felt. Ink is a rule on that force and on poses, not a fluid: a whole mark at 5 N or more with the die flat, a faint one below; it never runs out, transfers or blots. A mark is drawn as the stamp's framed word in its label colour (a real pad gives one colour). The book is one rigid block (4 mm, 90 g); the felt is a slab on a 4 N/mm spring; other parts are boxes under CAD visuals.
